A.explanation: A steady decrease would suggest a progressive wave losing energy with distance, not the fixed node-antinode pattern of a stationary wave.

B.explanation: Q moves through alternate nodes of near-zero amplitude and antinodes of maximum amplitude, so the detected amplitude rises and falls regularly.

C.explanation: A steady increase would suggest amplitude grows toward P, whereas a stationary wave has repeated maxima and minima along S to P.

D.explanation: Constant amplitude would occur for a single travelling wave of constant amplitude, not when incident and reflected waves superpose to give position-dependent amplitude.

hints: Notice the incident microwaves from S and the reflected microwaves from metal screen P overlap in the same region to form a stationary wave.
Recall a stationary wave has fixed nodes where amplitude is minimum and antinodes where amplitude is maximum, spaced by $\lambda/2$.
Use the fact that the wavelength is much smaller than distance SP, so Q moving slowly from S to P must pass through many successive nodes and antinodes.
walkthrough: The wave travelling from S to P reflects at the metal screen P, so two waves of the same wavelength travel in opposite directions between S and P.
Their superposition forms a stationary wave whose amplitude varies with position but not with time at a fixed point.
At nodes the two waves always cancel, giving near-zero detected amplitude, and at antinodes they reinforce, giving maximum amplitude.
Successive nodes are separated by $\lambda/2$, with an antinode midway between each pair, so amplitude varies periodically with distance.
Because $\lambda$ is much smaller than SP, there are many nodes and antinodes between S and P.
Detector Q moving at constant speed therefore samples a regularly repeating sequence of maxima and minima in signal amplitude. This is option B.
